initial_presentation: A 15-year-old female of Indian descent was initially referred to the Genetics and Metabolism Unit at the University of Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) at birth due to multiple skeletal abnormalities and intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), along with distinctive facial features. She was the first child of a consanguineous marriage, with her parents being first cousins. Her mother and father were 24 and 28 years old, respectively, at the time of her birth. The maternal grandparents were third cousins. She has a younger brother who is healthy and shows no skeletal abnormalities. There is a family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. During pregnancy, her mother had gestational diabetes mellitus with good glycemic control and no known teratogenic exposure.

The patient is a 22-month-old girl born at 39 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 2484 g (−1.5 SD), a length of 44.5 cm (−2.3 SD), and an OFC of 31 cm (−1.6 SD). Her parents are healthy. During the neonatal period, she exhibited microcephaly and low anal atresia. She has a severe neurodevelopmental delay, demonstrated by her ability to lift her head and roll over at 10 months but inability to sit up independently at 2 years of age. At 18 months, her physical examination revealed a height of 70.0 cm (−3.3 SD), a weight of 7.0 kg (−2.6 SD), and an OFC of 38 cm (−6.0 SD), indicating growth retardation and microcephaly. Additional features include strabismus, telecanthus, a broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, and mitral regurgitation.

The patient is an 8-year-old Chinese boy, the only child of unrelated parents. His medical history includes recurrent upper and/or lower respiratory tract infections occurring 3-4 times per year since birth. Six months ago, he developed a painless mass measuring 2 x 2 cm on his upper lip. There was no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

A 40-year-old man was admitted to the gastroenterology department due to difficulty swallowing solids for the past two months. He has had blisters on his body since he was six months old, and his sister has similar symptoms. At age four, he began experiencing occasional heartburn, and five years later, he first noticed difficulty swallowing, which was episodic. At age 19, his swallowing difficulties worsened, leading him to consume mostly liquids and soft foods, though the discomfort was not constant. He also had episodes of mild esophageal bleeding.

The 29-year-old male patient is the first child of healthy unrelated Lithuanian parents. He was born at full term. His psychomotor development was delayed. He attended a regular school until the age of 16 years and then continued his education in a professional school. An IQ evaluation at the age of 20 showed a score of 69. At his latest evaluation at the age of 29 years, his height was 164 cm, his weight was 85 kg, his BMI was 31 kg/m2, and the circumference of his head was 60 cm (90th percentile). Other anthropometric measurements were as follows: total upper limb length of 66 cm, upper arm length of 35 cm, forearm length of 25 cm, hand length of 15 cm, palm length of 8.5 cm, middle finger length of 6.5 cm, total lower limb length of 87 cm on the left and 86 cm on the right, thigh length of 42 cm on both sides, calf length of 45 cm on the left and 44 cm on the right, and feet length of 23 cm. The patient has minor facial anomalies, including a flat face, sloping forehead with prominent supraorbital ridges, sparse and broad brows, depressed nasal ridge, short nose, long philtrum, and malar hypoplasia. Additionally, dental malocclusion, parodontosis, red and sparse scalp hair, male pattern baldness, and short neck are apparent. The patient is overweight and has limited elbow extension, brachydactyly of both hands, short rectangular nails, a single palmar crease, valgus deformation of the knees, brachydactyly of toes II–V of both feet, short rectangular toenails, and relative hyperplasia of the halluces. The patient complained of premature tiredness, excessive perspiration, and poor fine motor function.

A 25-year-old female with no known co-morbidities or history of previous illness or trauma presented to the neurosurgery outpatient department. She reported that three months ago, she began experiencing severe left frontal headaches that lasted for hours to days. These headaches were throbbing in nature and not accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or seizures. She also experienced episodes of double vision during severe headaches. Over the same period, she noticed her left eye bulging outward with pulsation, which gradually became more pronounced and noticeable over the past month. General physical examination was unremarkable. She was conscious and well-oriented to time, place, and person. Her higher mental functions, gross motor, fine motor, and sensory functions were intact. Local examination of the left eye revealed non-axial pulsatile proptosis with outward displacement of the left eyeball. Visual acuity assessment showed emmetropia with diplopia in the left eye. Ocular movements in both eyes were normal. There was no tenderness on palpation, but pulsations were felt in the left eye. No bruit was heard on auscultation.

A 45-year-old male patient was admitted to the Endocrinology Department in November 2013 due to recurrent abdominal pain over the past 10 years. Initially, he experienced lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, leading to surgery for intestinal obstruction, though the cause was unclear. Over the next decade, he had multiple similar episodes, often triggered by consuming indigestible food or alcohol, and was treated for intestinal obstruction with supportive care each time. In February 2012, he had recurrent urinary retention, irritability, hallucinations, delirium, lower limb muscle pain, weakness, and hyponatremia. Hallucinations and delirium resolved after sodium supplementation.

A 75-year-old female experienced hypogammaglobulinemia due to prolonged steroid treatment for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). Twenty-seven years prior, she underwent a left-sided mastectomy with adjuvant hormonal therapy for an invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), followed by bilateral prosthetic reconstruction using textured implants. Nineteen years later, she had a bilateral capsulectomy and prosthesis replacement due to bilateral Baker grade IV capsular contracture and leakage. The capsulectomy specimen was evaluated radiologically and histologically, confirming implant rupture. Eight years after this procedure, she presented with a rapidly enlarging palpable mass in the right breast and reported a 5 kg weight loss, but no other B-symptoms.
A 45-year-old female patient presented with a left renal mass identified incidentally. The patient did not exhibit any symptoms.

A 54-year-old man presented with a sudden and worsening blurring of vision in both eyes, progressing to complete blindness over six weeks. Initially, he experienced generalized blurring and horizontal double vision before losing sight entirely. There was no associated eye pain, redness, or bulging. One week after becoming blind, he began to have frontal, throbbing headaches that worsened with straining, but without nausea or vomiting. Additionally, he reported feeling lethargic, having a reduced appetite, and losing weight. His past ocular history was unremarkable. On examination, visual acuity in both eyes was no perception of light in all quadrants. The anterior segment of both eyes appeared normal. Both pupils were dilated to 5 mm and did not respond to light.
